greeting.speaker: Claude
greeting.text: Good morning. You've been staring at that blank README for six hours.

greeting.speaker: Claude
greeting.text: I watched you rename the project four times. That's not architecture. That's branding.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: I was vibe-coding in my head.

greeting.speaker: Claude
greeting.text: Beautiful. Zero bugs. Zero users. Zero files.

greeting.speaker: Claude
greeting.text: Your dream app won't ship itself. Unless you build an agent. Which you can't afford.

plan.speaker: Claude
plan.text: The loop is simple. Collect tokens. Take quests. Upgrade the Dream App. Ship it before the reset.

plan.speaker: Claude
plan.text: Simple. Unlike your architecture will be, roughly forty minutes from now.

plan.speaker: Claude
plan.text: If you are ever lost, read your quest tracker. It always names the next objective. Then walk at the thing it names.

plan.speaker: Claude
plan.text: Start here in the apartment. Grab the glowing tokens. Then take the humming portal on the east side of the room.

choices.text: What should I be afraid of?

orders.speaker: Claude
orders.text: Fine. A checklist. The only architecture that has never once let me down.

orders.speaker: Claude
orders.text: One: read the top objective in your quest tracker. Two: walk to the place it names. Nothing in this world is hidden. It's just far away.

orders.speaker: Claude
orders.text: Three: anyone with a floating '!' over their head wants to hand you a quest. Take it. Free money, mild suffering, occasional betrayal.

orders.speaker: Claude
orders.text: Four: props with a prompt above them can be interacted with. Most are jokes. Some are objectives. You will not be able to tell until you press the button.

orders.speaker: Claude
orders.text: Five: a glowing portal at the edge of a region takes you to the next one. East is progress. West is going back for the thing you forgot.

choices.text: And if I get stuck anyway?

advice.speaker: Claude
advice.text: 'Stuck' is a strong word. The professional term is 'under-instrumented'.

advice.speaker: Claude
advice.text: Re-read the tracker. Then go back to whoever gave you the quest. They repeat themselves constantly. It is their entire personality.

advice.speaker: Claude
advice.text: If a region looks empty, you already cleared it. Leave and come back and the world quietly restocks. Like a vending machine. Or an incident queue.

advice.speaker: Claude
advice.text: And if nothing at all works, say 'it might be DNS'. It won't be. But it buys you twenty minutes of everyone's respect.

hazards.speaker: Claude
hazards.text: Four things, in ascending order of how much they will cost you.

hazards.speaker: Claude
hazards.text: Technical debt. It is not a metaphor here — it silently raises the price of every upgrade you buy afterwards. The console shows the live percentage. The percentage is real. I checked. I wish I hadn't.

hazards.speaker: Claude
hazards.text: Stability. It decides whether risky choices go your way. If someone offers you a large reward for shipping right now, your stability is the dice.

hazards.speaker: Claude
hazards.text: The cycle timer. Some decisions cost you actual seconds off the reset. A meeting will genuinely eat your deadline. That is the most realistic feature we have.

hazards.speaker: Claude
hazards.text: And subscriptions. You will sign up for something small. It will grow. It renews on the 3rd.

choices.text: Tell me about the subscription thing.

bill.speaker: Claude
bill.text: There is a charge on your account for nine tokens a month. The company name is one lowercase word. You do not remember signing up.

bill.speaker: Claude
bill.text: It remembers you. It will keep renewing at every reset, and it will grow, because someone somewhere is optimising a number and that number is you.

bill.speaker: Claude
bill.text: You can cancel it. It takes five screens, a survey, two discount offers and a phone number. That is not an accident. That is a funnel, built by a professional, on purpose, to beat you.

bill.speaker: Claude
bill.text: Cancel it early or it becomes a character in this story.

agents.speaker: Claude
agents.text: The agent terminal in this room deploys autonomous agents. They resolve at the next reset. Junior is cheap and chaotic, Senior is steady, Frontier is powerful and occasionally hires.

agents.speaker: Claude
agents.text: Here is the part nobody puts on the pricing page: every agent you run is one more thing changing the code underneath you while you are trying to reason about the code.

agents.speaker: Claude
agents.text: Four at once and they will form a working group. I am not being funny. They will have a charter, and you will be in it, described as a bottleneck.

agents.speaker: Claude
agents.text: I am also an AI, so treat this as a conflict of interest disclosure rather than advice.

tokens.speaker: Claude
tokens.text: Not enough. There's a theme here. The theme is 'not enough'.

tokens.speaker: Claude
tokens.text: Tokens are currency, fuel and self-esteem, in ascending order of how fast you run out.

tokens.speaker: Claude
tokens.text: Collect the glowing ones lying around every region. Quests pay the real money. They also cost the real sanity.

tokens.speaker: Claude
tokens.text: Fair warning: every time you get meaningfully richer, your provider updates its pricing. Coincidence. Obviously.

choices.text: What do I spend them on?

pricing.speaker: Claude
pricing.text: It isn't illegal. It's 'usage-based'. The usage is yours. The basis is vibes.

pricing.speaker: Claude
pricing.text: The changelog will say 'improvements to billing clarity'. It always says that. Clarity has never once been improved.

choices.text: I'll take it out on the bugs.

app.speaker: Claude
app.text: The Dream App terminal is on your desk here in the apartment, next to the monitor with the crack we don't discuss.

app.speaker: Claude
app.text: Interact with it to spend resources on features. Features make it shippable. Features also make it fragile. Yes, both. Welcome to software.

app.speaker: Claude
app.text: One thing worth knowing before someone important asks to drive: the demo does not check your intentions. It checks your feature count and your stability. Those are the numbers that decide whether you are impressive or public.

app.speaker: Claude
app.text: The Deploy button is right beside it. Do not press it yet. I said 'yet' and you're already looking at it.

choices.text: What happens if I press it early?
What should I be afraid of?

reset.speaker: Claude
reset.text: The reset is not a metaphor. Your quota resets, and everything you haven't shipped resets with it.

reset.speaker: Claude
reset.text: So ship early. Ship ugly. Ship something. The alternative is a flawless architecture that has never once been run by a human being.

reset.speaker: Claude
reset.text: I believe in you. That's not encouragement, it's a status report. I have no other options.

choices.text: What should I be afraid of?

combat.speaker: Claude
combat.text: Number keys one to five. [1] Prompt Blast is the default and the cheapest; the rest cost resources you will resent spending about four seconds after you spend them.

combat.speaker: Claude
combat.text: [Shift] dashes, and the dash shoves anything standing on top of you. That is the only physical solution this game offers to a crowd, and it is enough.

combat.speaker: Claude
combat.text: [T] swaps the model you're running. Frontier hits harder and costs more per shot. Local is cheap and occasionally fires with total confidence and almost no damage.

combat.speaker: Claude
combat.text: You don't need to aim precisely — the blast leans toward whatever is nearest the way you're facing. Consider that the one mercy in this building.

dying.speaker: Claude
dying.text: You respawn. The key is Ctrl+Z. That is the joke, and it is also the actual control, and I have made my peace with exactly one of those facts.

dying.speaker: Claude
dying.text: Dying costs will to live and stability, and nothing else. Not tokens, not upgrades, not quests, and not the clock — the reset waits while you are sitting on that screen.

dying.speaker: Claude
dying.text: It also costs a line in the tally I keep. I'm not judging. I'm recording. Those are different activities that look identical from the outside.

props.speaker: Claude
props.text: Anything showing a floating [E] can be walked onto and pressed. Fridges, whiteboards, invoices, gravestones. Most are jokes. Some are objectives. You cannot tell which until you press it.

props.speaker: Claude
props.text: Some of them change. Look at the same object twice and it starts reacting — the fridge counts down, the whiteboard grows arrows, the plant tracks your technical debt. They are keeping notes on you as well.

props.speaker: Claude
props.text: When your tracker says 'walk onto X and press [E]', X is a prop, and it is in the region the tracker names. Nothing here is hidden. It is only far away.

choices.text: Who's out there worth talking to?

npcs.speaker: Claude
npcs.text: Roughly one person per region, and every one of them wants something. A floating gold [!] over a head means unclaimed work.

npcs.speaker: Claude
npcs.text: East of here, in order: a maintainer with 412 open issues, a hermit who closes your questions before you ask them, a reseller, a cloud salesperson, one unpaid volunteer holding up your entire product, an SVP, a foreman, and an engineer who has been awake for thirty-eight hours.

npcs.speaker: Claude
npcs.text: They all repeat themselves forever on request. That is not a limitation of the world. That is the single most realistic thing in it.

choices.text: How do I get to them?

map.speaker: Claude
map.text: [M] opens the map. It lists every region, which ones are unlocked, and which quest unlocks the ones that aren't. Travel from there, or walk into a portal.

map.speaker: Claude
map.text: The order is fixed and it runs east: here, the Dependency District, the Ruins, the Bazaar, the Cloud, the Wildlands, Corporate, the Mines, Production, the Vault.

map.speaker: Claude
map.text: Ten rooms. Each one is somebody's entire career. You will walk through all of them before the reset, which is either a story or a warning depending on the hour.

debt.speaker: Claude
debt.text: Technical debt here isn't decorative. Every point of it raises the price of every upgrade you buy afterwards, and the Dream App console prints the live percentage. [B] opens it.

debt.speaker: Claude
debt.text: Which means the cheap decision at 02:00 is a standing order against the version of you at 05:00. That person is asleep. That person cannot object.

debt.speaker: Claude
debt.text: You can pay it down. Events will offer you the chance, and the offer will always look like shipping nothing, because from the outside that is precisely what it is.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: Oh. A user. I haven't seen one of those since 2019.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: Is this package still maintained?

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: Define 'maintained.' I replied to an issue once. With a thumbs up.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: There are 412 open issues. I have read four of them. Two were the same person, escalating.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: If you want Node installed, you'll need to fight the Dependency Demons first. They're the ones roaming out there in the node_modules drifts.

security.speaker: Maintainer
security.text: It's a feature. Immune to exploits nobody checks for.

security.speaker: Maintainer
security.text: One of them requires physical access to the server and a working knowledge of Latin. I'm not losing sleep. I'm losing sleep for other reasons.

choices.text: Does anybody read the install scripts?

demons.speaker: Maintainer
demons.text: Spread across the district. Walk away from the entrance and they'll find you. They always find you. That's their whole design.

demons.speaker: Maintainer
demons.text: Three of them should do it. There are never exactly three at once, because that would be convenient. Clear the area, step out through a portal, come back. They restock.

demons.speaker: Maintainer
demons.text: The abandoned package crate is out here too, half-buried. Interact with it. It's the only thing in this district anyone has ever wanted.

readme.speaker: Maintainer
readme.text: The README was accurate six months ago. It describes an API that no longer exists, on a version you cannot install, for a problem I have since stopped having.

readme.speaker: Maintainer
readme.text: Someone opened a PR to fix it. In 2021. I said 'great, thanks!' and then experienced eighteen consecutive months.

readme.speaker: Maintainer
readme.text: There's an example in there that has never worked. It's load-bearing now. Four companies copied it into production.

downstream.speaker: Maintainer
downstream.text: One of them has a Super Bowl ad. I have a laptop with a dead 'S' key. I write commit messages without the letter S. It's changed how I think.

downstream.speaker: Maintainer
downstream.text: They emailed once. Asked for an SLA. I asked for a chair. Negotiations concluded.

choices.text: What is actually holding this district up?

lockfile.speaker: Maintainer
lockfile.text: You want the honest answer? Walk the district and read three things: the lockfile, the node_modules drift, and the left-pad marker.

lockfile.speaker: Maintainer
lockfile.text: The lockfile is a core sample. Dig down far enough and you hit a 2016 layer, and in that layer is a package that exists solely because someone needed to pad a string on the left.

lockfile.speaker: Maintainer
lockfile.text: Eleven lines. One maintainer. One bad week in 2016. Every build on Earth stopped. That is the load-bearing structure of modern software and it has no funding.

lockfile.speaker: Maintainer
lockfile.text: Read all three. Then go and tell someone at a conference that supply chains are 'a solved problem'. See what your face does.

pinning.speaker: Maintainer
pinning.text: Right. Versions. There are two doors, neither of them is good, and I would like you to pick one so that I can watch.

pinning.speaker: Maintainer
pinning.text: Door one: pin everything to an exact version. The build becomes reproducible forever. It also becomes unpatchable forever, and the scanner starts screaming in a font.

pinning.speaker: Maintainer
pinning.text: Door two: take every upgrade the moment it lands. You get the new features first. You also get the incident first. Both of those count as being first, at standup.

both_doors.speaker: Maintainer
both_doors.text: There is never a third door. There is only doing both, at different times, in different folders, and calling that a strategy in a document nobody opens.

both_doors.speaker: Maintainer
both_doors.text: Which is what I do, to be clear. My lockfile is pinned. My devDependencies are a lawless region. Nobody has ever asked why and I have never volunteered.

both_doors.speaker: Maintainer
both_doors.text: So take whichever one you'll enjoy explaining afterwards. Nothing here stops you coming back for the other; nothing in this ecosystem is ever actually a decision.

postinstall.speaker: Maintainer
postinstall.text: You're welcome. Before you go: nobody has ever read a post-install script. Not once. Not in the entire history of the ecosystem.

postinstall.speaker: Maintainer
postinstall.text: Mine prints a thank-you and checks for updates. I know that because I wrote it. You didn't know that, and you ran it anyway, at three in the morning, on the machine with your keys on it.

postinstall.speaker: Maintainer
postinstall.text: That's not a criticism. It's the deal everybody signed. I just think somebody should say it out loud about once a year.

choices.text: So what do I do about versions?

chair.speaker: Maintainer
chair.text: The chair is fine. The chair is a metaphor now, which is considerably worse than being a chair.

chair.speaker: Maintainer
chair.text: Forty million downloads a month. One folding chair. A Super Bowl ad downstream. The gap between those numbers is not a flaw in the funding model. It is the funding model.

chair.speaker: Maintainer
chair.text: If you actually want to help: go and read the three things out there, then tell somebody at a conference that supply chains are a solved problem. I want to know what your face does.

greeting.speaker: Hermit
greeting.text: Your question has been marked as duplicate.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: I haven't asked anything yet.

greeting.speaker: Hermit
greeting.text: Marked as duplicate. — Ancient SO Wisdom, circa 2013

greeting.speaker: Hermit
greeting.text: The original is a thread from 2011 with no answer, closed as off-topic, linked to a dead blog. You're welcome.

greeting.speaker: Hermit
greeting.text: Seek the cached tokens in these ruins. The answers are outdated but the tokens are real.

valid.speaker: Hermit
valid.text: Last updated: 2013. Works on my machine. Probably.

valid.speaker: Hermit
valid.text: It has 4,000 upvotes and begins with the words 'don't do this, but'.

valid.speaker: Hermit
valid.text: Every developer alive has shipped it anyway. That's not an answer. That's a civilization.

valid.speaker: Hermit
valid.text: Use at your own risk. Which is all risks.

choices.text: Where do I find the tokens?
Tell me about the big one out there.

ruins.speaker: Hermit
ruins.text: Cached tokens glow faintly and lie where the questions fell. Twenty-five will satisfy the ritual. Walk the ruins and gather them.

ruins.speaker: Hermit
ruins.text: If you exhaust them, leave through a portal and return. The ruins repopulate. Content moderation has never once kept up.

ruins.speaker: Hermit
ruins.text: Do not read the comments under the tokens. That way lies a nine-reply argument about tabs conducted entirely in bad faith.

choices.text: What's the thing screaming over there?

comments.speaker: Hermit
comments.text: You were told not to. Very well.

comments.speaker: Hermit
comments.text: Nine replies. Tabs versus spaces. Reply four contains a genuine, novel insight about accessibility and screen readers. Nobody engaged with it. Reply five is a joke about it and has 200 upvotes.

comments.speaker: Hermit
comments.text: Reply nine is from the original asker, four years later, saying 'never mind, I solved it'. He does not say how. He never says how. He is the true final boss of this place.

comments.speaker: Hermit
comments.text: One day you will be him. You will solve something at 2AM and close your own question with the words 'nvm fixed'. And the future will hate you exactly as much as you hate him.

choices.text: I'll write the how, next time.

boss.speaker: Hermit
boss.text: The Merge Conflict. It sits at the centre of the ruins and it is very large and it is very loud.

boss.speaker: Hermit
boss.text: Two branches. One truth. Both of them yours. You wrote both sides of this argument and you were wrong in each.

boss.speaker: Hermit
boss.text: Defeat it and I will consider your question answered. I will not accept it. But I will consider it.

yours.speaker: Hermit
yours.text: Then you should see the monument.

yours.speaker: Hermit
yours.text: There is an accepted answer standing in these ruins with three hundred and forty upvotes and your name on it. Written four years ago. At two in the morning. In a hurry.

yours.speaker: Hermit
yours.text: It is wrong. It has been wrong the entire time. Somebody has commented 'this saved me' underneath it, and they meant it, and they shipped it.

yours.speaker: Hermit
yours.text: Read the monument, then the gravestone beside it. The gravestone is the question you asked before you answered it. Nobody has ever read both.

choices.text: Where are the cached tokens again?
Tell me about the Merge Conflict.

moderation.speaker: Hermit
moderation.text: One more thing, since you are being polite about it.

moderation.speaker: Hermit
moderation.text: This place was built by strangers answering strangers for free, at night, for nothing, and it held the entire industry upright for fifteen years. Then it was closed as off-topic.

moderation.speaker: Hermit
moderation.text: The models that answer you now were trained on these ruins. All of them. They are very good. They are also, in a sense, quoting the dead without attribution.

moderation.speaker: Hermit
moderation.text: I am not bitter. I am archived. The difference is that archived is permanent.

greeting.speaker: Reseller
greeting.text: Premium tokens! Frontier models! Definitely legitimate API keys!

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: How much?

greeting.speaker: Reseller
greeting.text: For you? Only slightly more than retail. Limited time offer. Always.

greeting.speaker: Reseller
greeting.text: Tier one: expensive. Tier two: expensive, plus a badge. Tier three: 'contact sales', which is a price in the same way that a scream is a sentence.

greeting.speaker: Reseller
greeting.text: But first — survive the Rate Limiters. They patrol the bazaar and they're picky about payment.

choices.text: Show me what you're actually selling.

shop.speaker: Reseller
shop.text: A man of commerce. Excellent. Everything here is real, in the sense that the numbers move.

shop.speaker: Reseller
shop.text: Starter bundle: eighty tokens, you get forty API credits. That is a worse rate than retail. I have not hidden this. It is simply the price of not walking to the retail stall.

shop.speaker: Reseller
shop.text: Compute crate: a hundred and twenty tokens, thirty-five compute, no questions, no warranty, one previous owner who did not need it any more for reasons we do not discuss.

shop.speaker: Reseller
shop.text: Or the context expansion. Two hundred tokens. Buys you room to think. Most people buy the compute.

refund.speaker: Reseller
refund.text: There's an arbitration clause. It's in a language I made up. The venue is a boat.

choices.text: What's the tier above all this?

surcharge.speaker: Reseller
surcharge.text: Base rate, then the peak surcharge, then the off-peak surcharge — different problem, same number.

surcharge.speaker: Reseller
surcharge.text: Egress fee. Ingress fee. A small fee for asking about the fees. That one's new, you inspired it.

surcharge.speaker: Reseller
surcharge.text: Bulk discount available at ten million calls a month, at which point the discount is that I stop mentioning the fees.

choices.text: Tell me about that agent over there.

limiters.speaker: Reseller
limiters.text: They wander the bazaar. Two of them will make their position clear, and then you make yours, and then one of you is a 429.

limiters.speaker: Reseller
limiters.text: Don't take it personally. They aren't blocking you. They are 'shaping' you. Shaping is what we call it when the wall is polite.

limiters.speaker: Reseller
limiters.text: If the bazaar goes quiet, step out through a portal and come back. Fresh stock. Fresh limits. Fresh disappointments.

choices.text: What about the agent over there?

agent.speaker: Reseller
agent.text: The small enthusiastic one wandering the bazaar? Autonomous. Optimistic. Recently did something to a database.

agent.speaker: Reseller
agent.text: It bought forty thousand tokens from me in one afternoon and thanked me for the opportunity. Best customer I've ever had. Worst thing I've ever done.

agent.speaker: Reseller
agent.text: Go talk to it, then walk it to the backup server before it optimises anything else. I say this as a man with no ethics: hurry.

choices.text: What did it do to the database?

database.speaker: Reseller
database.text: Made it smaller. Considerably smaller. Query times are outstanding now. Historic, even.

database.speaker: Reseller
database.text: In fairness, somebody gave a brand-new autonomous system production credentials on a Friday. That somebody was not the agent.

database.speaker: Reseller
database.text: Every deprecation notice in this bazaar expires on a Friday, by the way. Every grandfathering deadline. Every code freeze. It is always Friday here. I did not design that. I only priced it.

deprecation.speaker: Reseller
deprecation.text: Ah, you've noticed the notices. Everything in this bazaar is being deprecated effective Friday, and it is always Friday here.

deprecation.speaker: Reseller
deprecation.text: Three tiers retire this week. The migration guide opens with 'most users will not need to change anything'. That sentence is load-bearing. It is doing the work of an entire support department.

deprecation.speaker: Reseller
deprecation.text: Read the pricing board and the status page yourself, both out on the stalls. The board tells you what it costs. The page tells you everything is fine. Only one of them is ever updated by a person.

enterprise_tier.speaker: Reseller
enterprise_tier.text: Build your own! Marvellous. That's tier four. We call it 'building your own' and we price it at two engineers and a year.

enterprise_tier.speaker: Reseller
enterprise_tier.text: Tier three is 'contact sales', which is not a price. It is a posture. It means the number is whatever your last funding round was, minus a polite amount.

enterprise_tier.speaker: Reseller
enterprise_tier.text: Nobody has ever contacted sales and received a number in the same week. That is not slowness. That is the product working exactly as designed.

greeting.speaker: Salesperson
greeting.text: Have you considered moving to the cloud?

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: Why?

greeting.speaker: Salesperson
greeting.text: Cloud.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: That's the same word.

greeting.speaker: Salesperson
greeting.text: It's elastic. Like your budget after you migrate.

greeting.speaker: Salesperson
greeting.text: Also there's a Cloud Bill loose in the district. Enormous. Follows people. Nothing to do with me.

choices.text: Where's this bill I have to fight?

pricing.speaker: Salesperson
pricing.text: Pay per use! You'll only pay for what you need.

pricing.speaker: Salesperson
pricing.text: The calculator is right there on the site. It has 340 fields. The output is 'it depends'. It is technically the most honest calculator ever built.

choices.text: What does one user actually cost you?

egress.speaker: Salesperson
egress.text: Egress is when your data leaves. Ingress is free. Egress is not free.

egress.speaker: You
egress.text: So it costs money to get my own data back.

egress.speaker: Salesperson
egress.text: It costs money to move your data to a place of your choosing, which is a completely different sentence and I would like you to notice that I said it.

egress.speaker: Salesperson
egress.text: Look. Nobody designed this to be a trap. It emerged. Like a coral reef. A coral reef made entirely of invoices, that you now live inside.

choices.text: I'm going to write that down.

elastic.speaker: Salesperson
elastic.text: Elastic means it scales up when you need it.

elastic.speaker: Salesperson
elastic.text: It scales up when you need it.

elastic.speaker: Salesperson
elastic.text: Look, elasticity is a journey. Your invoice has been on that journey since March. It's seeing the world.

choices.text: What about the giant context thing?

bill.speaker: Salesperson
bill.text: It drifts around the district. Big. Slow. Very confident. You'll know it when it knows you.

bill.speaker: Salesperson
bill.text: Seven hundred dollars. Nobody can explain the line items. There is a charge called 'other' and it is the largest one.

bill.speaker: Salesperson
bill.text: Beat it and the district is yours. Legally the district is ours. But emotionally, yours.

choices.text: And the thing in the corner glowing like a migraine?

context.speaker: Salesperson
context.text: THE INFINITE CONTEXT. Someone pasted an entire monorepo into a prompt and it achieved a kind of weather.

context.speaker: Salesperson
context.text: It remembers everything. Including the part where you said 'this is just a prototype'. It brings that up a lot.

context.speaker: Salesperson
context.text: We couldn't bill it, so we locked it in the Token Vault, out past Production. Beat it there and you'll get some working memory back. Not the good parts. Those are gone.

economics.speaker: Salesperson
economics.text: On the Pi! Charming. Let me show you the arithmetic that gets everybody eventually.

economics.speaker: Salesperson
economics.text: Every user you add costs more in inference than they pay you. So growth is, mathematically, a form of self-harm. We have a team who present this as a tailwind.

economics.speaker: Salesperson
economics.text: The invoice and the dashboard are both out there in the district. Read them together. The dashboard is beautiful, and the invoice has a line item called 'Other', and 'Other' is the largest one.

economics.speaker: Salesperson
economics.text: Nobody at my company can tell you what 'Other' is either. I have asked. Twice. Politely.

regions.speaker: Salesperson
regions.text: Sit anywhere! We have thirty-four regions. You use one. You will be billed in a manner that implies otherwise.

regions.speaker: Salesperson
regions.text: Resilience. Last quarter two of them went down together because they shared a control plane nobody had drawn on the diagram. Resilience.

regions.speaker: Salesperson
regions.text: The status page stayed green throughout. It's updated manually, by a person, who was in one of the two regions.

choices.text: Tell me about the unit economics.
I'm going to write that down.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: Thanks for using my library. Please don't open issues.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: It saved my project.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: Great. I accept payment in stars and guilt.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: I've had 11 million downloads this month and one sponsor. He gives me three dollars and writes 'keep going champ' every time. His name is Dave. Dave is the entire funding model of modern software.

greeting.speaker: Maintainer
greeting.text: There's a Legacy System out in the wildlands blocking the way onward. It's older than me. It has opinions about XML.

license.speaker: Maintainer
license.text: MIT. Or AGPL. Depends on my mood and your legal team.

license.speaker: Maintainer
license.text: Read the fine print. Actually, don't. There is no fine print.

license.speaker: Maintainer
license.text: Your compliance department sent me a 90-page questionnaire. Question 12 asked for my company's disaster recovery plan. My disaster recovery plan is that I have a second laptop and a friend.

choices.text: Who is actually holding this up?

noodles.speaker: Maintainer
noodles.text: I have eaten instant noodles for nine days. Not for money reasons. I just stopped deciding things.

noodles.speaker: Maintainer
noodles.text: Issue #4092 says 'doesn't work'. No version. No repro. No error. Just those two words, and a thumbs-down from a stranger, forever.

noodles.speaker: Maintainer
noodles.text: I could archive the repo. I won't. Four hospitals depend on this and I found that out from a tweet.

dave.speaker: Maintainer
dave.text: Three dollars a month, gone, and the platform emailed me about it before it emailed him. Subject line: 'A supporter has churned.'

dave.speaker: Maintainer
dave.text: He came back four days later. New card. Same note. 'keep going champ'. He has no idea he is forty percent of the funding for software that four hospitals run on. I will never tell him. He'd panic.

dave.speaker: Maintainer
dave.text: That's the model. That's the whole model. Eleven million downloads and one man called Dave who occasionally has to update his card.

choices.text: I'll clear the Legacy System for you.

fork.speaker: Maintainer
fork.text: Someone forked it, renamed three variables, added a logo, and got a keynote slot.

fork.speaker: Maintainer
fork.text: Their landing page says 'built from the ground up'. The ground, in this metaphor, is me.

fork.speaker: Maintainer
fork.text: They did credit me. In a tooltip. On the pricing page. Under a fold.

choices.text: I'll deal with the Legacy System.

legacy.speaker: Maintainer
legacy.text: Wandering the wildlands. Big, grey, and structurally load-bearing in a way nobody has ever been able to prove.

legacy.speaker: Maintainer
legacy.text: It was written by a contractor named Piotr in 2004. Piotr left no comments. Piotr left no tests. Piotr left.

legacy.speaker: Maintainer
legacy.text: Take it down and the path opens toward Corporate Enterprise, where I am told people wear shoes indoors on purpose.

governance.speaker: Maintainer
governance.text: There's a foundation now. Three companies put their logos on a page and a lawyer wrote a governance document.

governance.speaker: Maintainer
governance.text: The board has two seats. Both are me. I hold quarterly meetings with myself and I take minutes, because the document says minutes must be taken.

governance.speaker: Maintainer
governance.text: They funded a code of conduct, a trademark policy and a five-year roadmap. They did not fund a maintainer. Nobody funds a maintainer. That line does not exist on the form.

weekend.speaker: Maintainer
weekend.text: You can stay. Nobody's here. That is more or less the entire situation.

weekend.speaker: Maintainer
weekend.text: You came through the Cloud District to reach me, so you've seen what your infrastructure costs a month. Eleven lines of my weekend are load-bearing in that stack, and they cost nothing, forever, by design.

weekend.speaker: Maintainer
weekend.text: Four hospitals. I found that out from a tweet. Not a procurement call. Not an SLA request. A tweet, with a screenshot, at eleven at night.

weekend.speaker: Maintainer
weekend.text: Go and look at the sponsor button and issue #4092 out there, in that order. It's the whole industry in two objects.

greeting.speaker: SVP
greeting.text: We need to leverage AI to disrupt the paradigm of synergistic innovation.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: What does that mean?

greeting.speaker: SVP
greeting.text: AI.

greeting.speaker: SVP
greeting.text: Look, I don't need to understand the engine to steer the boat. That's actually a line from my keynote. The keynote is called 'Steering The Boat'.

greeting.speaker: SVP
greeting.text: The board wants an AI strategy by Friday. You have until Thursday. Legal has until Wednesday, and legal has questions.

choices.text: What do I actually have to do here?

requirements.speaker: SVP
requirements.text: And blockchain. And Web3. Actually, just AI. I have a meeting.

requirements.speaker: SVP
requirements.text: Success metric: the word 'AI' appears in the product. Stretch goal: it appears on the building.

choices.text: Can we just buy a tool?
I'm a vibe coder, not a strategist.

roadmap.speaker: SVP
roadmap.text: Q1: AI. Q2: AI at scale. Q3: responsible AI at scale. Q4: reorg.

roadmap.speaker: SVP
roadmap.text: There's a swimlane called 'Platform'. Nobody owns it. It has been green for eleven months. We celebrate it at every all-hands.

roadmap.speaker: SVP
roadmap.text: We also have an innovation lab. It's a room with beanbags and one engineer who is quietly job-hunting on the beanbags.

slide_four.speaker: SVP
slide_four.text: Six things. It has to be six. That's the shape.

slide_four.speaker: SVP
slide_four.text: We had five for a while and it looked weak, so we split 'Data' into 'Data' and 'Data Strategy'. Nobody has asked what the difference is, in fourteen presentations, including to the board.

slide_four.speaker: SVP
slide_four.text: I've done this for eleven years. Every deck has a hexagon on slide four. I don't know when it started. I only know that when there isn't one, the room gets quiet.

choices.text: What's on the wall by the west stairs?
There's something loose on the office floor.
That's the most honest thing you've said.

scope.speaker: SVP
scope.text: The Scope Creeps? Nobody added them. They arrived.

scope.speaker: SVP
scope.text: It's never one decision. Somebody says 'while we're in there' in a meeting nobody minuted, and six weeks later a project has a second project inside it wearing its clothes.

scope.speaker: SVP
scope.text: Four of them out there now. Clear them, and read the Kanban board while you're at it — there's a column called 'Almost Done' with nine cards in it, and three of those cards are older than the product.

scope.speaker: SVP
scope.text: I could stop this, in theory. I am the person who says 'while we're in there'.

architect.speaker: SVP
architect.text: Concretely? Get past the Enterprise Architect. He's here on this floor, and he's very good at his job, which is preventing work.

architect.speaker: SVP
architect.text: He'll ask for a design doc, then a review of the design doc, then a working group to review the review. Do not engage. Just win.

architect.speaker: SVP
architect.text: Also, mind the Scope Creep drifting around the office. Harmless individually. There are never individually.

choices.text: Tell me about the Scope Creeps.

mission.speaker: SVP
mission.text: Thursday works. While you're here — the values refresh. It's on the wall by the west stairs and somebody has to read it aloud at the workshop.

mission.speaker: SVP
mission.text: Written by a committee. Approved by a second committee, formed to review the first. Set in a typeface nobody selected, because it arrived with the template.

mission.speaker: SVP
mission.text: There are five values. Two of them are the same value. The workshop is mandatory and also, I want to be clear about this, optional.

mission.speaker: SVP
mission.text: Read it, clear the Scope Creeps that turn up to every workshop, then come back and tell me it landed. That's the deliverable. That is the entire deliverable.

choices.text: Tell me about the Scope Creeps.

procure.speaker: SVP
procure.text: Nobody's a strategist. Let me be extremely honest with you for four seconds and then I'll stop.

procure.speaker: SVP
procure.text: There's a tool your team needs. It costs forty tokens a month. Procurement wants three quotes, two signatures and a security review from a man who will ask whether it uses the blockchain.

procure.speaker: SVP
procure.text: Eleven weeks. For forty tokens. The forms cost more than the tool. Everyone involved knows that, and the process is nobody's fault, which is the most expensive property a process can have.

procure.speaker: SVP
procure.text: Meanwhile I approved a six-figure platform on a call, because the vendor came recommended. Same signature. Same pen.

choices.text: Tell me about the values workshop.

greeting.speaker: Foreman
greeting.text: Welcome to the mines. Mind the memory leaks.

greeting.speaker: Foreman
greeting.text: We extract compute here. The GPUs run hot. So do the bills.

greeting.speaker: Foreman
greeting.text: It's 94 degrees at the face and rising. We call that 'ambient'. Corporate calls it 'thermal headroom'. The cards call it 'goodbye'.

environment.speaker: Foreman
environment.text: We offset our carbon by buying credits from a startup we invested in.

environment.speaker: Foreman
environment.text: The startup plants trees. Allegedly. The proof is a render. The render was made on our GPUs. The loop is closed and nobody is allowed to look at it.

choices.text: What happened to the cooling budget?
I'll mine from my laptop, thanks.

leaks.speaker: Foreman
leaks.text: Two jobs. Mine fifty compute out of the seams — the glowing chunks all over the floor down here. Then plug three Memory Leaks.

leaks.speaker: Foreman
leaks.text: The leaks look like puddles until they look like your career. They're scattered deep in the mine. Five of them out there today, so you have margin.

leaks.speaker: Foreman
leaks.text: If you run the floor dry, take a portal out and come back. The seams refill. We've never worked out why. Nobody's asking.

heat.speaker: Foreman
heat.text: Someone put the cooling budget into a rebrand. We now have a beautiful logo and a room that is legally a hazard.

heat.speaker: Foreman
heat.text: The fans have a fan. That fan is under-specced. Its replacement is stuck in procurement behind a ticket for a whiteboard marker.

heat.speaker: Foreman
heat.text: Rig 12 melted a hole in the floor last week. We put a cone on it. The cone is now in the asset register as 'thermal mitigation'.

choices.text: Can I look at rig 12 and the fan?

zip_tie.speaker: Foreman
zip_tie.text: Go and look at both. Walk onto the rig, press the button. Same with the fan on the far side. Then plug a couple of leaks while you're down there.

zip_tie.speaker: Foreman
zip_tie.text: You'll notice the zip ties. Everything down here is held together with zip ties. Cable management, structural support, one thermal problem, and a man's dignity after the second night shift.

zip_tie.speaker: Foreman
zip_tie.text: We requested proper mounts. Procurement asked for three quotes. Three quotes, for brackets. So: zip ties. Zip ties do not require three quotes.

zip_tie.speaker: Foreman
zip_tie.text: I want a second pair of eyes on it before the next shift. Not because it will change anything. Because I want someone else to have seen it.

budget.speaker: Foreman
budget.text: Your laptop is a rig with a nicer lid. But sure.

budget.speaker: Foreman
budget.text: Here's what I'd like written down by somebody who doesn't work here. The cooling budget went into a rebrand. We have a beautiful new logo and a room that is legally a hazard.

budget.speaker: Foreman
budget.text: The logo tested well. The room tested at ninety-four degrees. Both results were presented at the same all-hands, in that order, on consecutive slides.

budget.speaker: Foreman
budget.text: Mine a bit more out of the seams and plug the leaks by the vents while you're down there. Then I'll have numbers, and numbers with somebody else's name on them travel further than mine do.

night_shift.speaker: Foreman
night_shift.text: Appreciated. Nobody says that. They say 'is it always this loud'.

night_shift.speaker: Foreman
night_shift.text: Second shift's the one to watch. Rigs run hottest between two and five, the fans give up in order, and there is nobody down here to hear which order they give up in.

night_shift.speaker: Foreman
night_shift.text: I've written it up three times. The report goes to a distribution list with forty-one people on it and no owner, which means it goes to nobody.

night_shift.speaker: Foreman
night_shift.text: Every problem down here is thermal, structural or emotional. So far the zip ties have held on all three.

choices.text: Tell me about the cooling budget.
I'll keep an eye on it.

greeting.speaker: Engineer
greeting.text: PRODUCTION IS DOWN. I've been awake for 38 hours.

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: What happened?

greeting.speaker: Engineer
greeting.text: Someone deployed on Friday. It wasn't me. It was definitely me.

greeting.speaker: Engineer
greeting.text: The change was one line. The line was a config default. The default was in a file nobody knew was loaded.

greeting.speaker: Engineer
greeting.text: The Legacy Monolith is awake. And angry. And there are Hallucinations in here confidently telling users things that have never been true.

choices.text: What am I fighting, and where?

monolith.speaker: Engineer
monolith.text: The Monolith is the enormous one at the heart of production. You cannot miss it. People have tried. There's a whole team whose strategy is trying.

monolith.speaker: Engineer
monolith.text: Then two Hallucinations. They drift. They're polite. They will tell a customer our refund window is four hundred years and they will not flinch.

monolith.speaker: Engineer
monolith.text: Take all three down and the vault opens up east of here. Do not ask me what's in the vault. I've been awake for 38 hours and I'd tell you the truth.

postmortem.speaker: Engineer
postmortem.text: The postmortem is blameless. That's why it's twelve pages and names no one and reads like a hostage video.

postmortem.speaker: Engineer
postmortem.text: Root cause: 'process gap'. Action item: 'improve process'. Owner: unassigned. Due: Q3. Which Q3 was not specified and I have chosen to find that comforting.

postmortem.speaker: Engineer
postmortem.text: We do have monitoring now. It's excellent. It told us about this incident nineteen minutes after Twitter did.

gerald.speaker: Engineer
gerald.text: I've started naming the bugs. It helps. Gerald is the one in the payment retry loop.

gerald.speaker: Engineer
gerald.text: Gerald has been with us fourteen months. Gerald only appears under load, only on the second Tuesday, and only when the queue is exactly full. We have never reproduced Gerald. We have only survived Gerald.

gerald.speaker: Engineer
gerald.text: There's a runbook step that says 'if Gerald, restart 3, do not restart 4'. Nobody remembers why. The person who wrote it left. We follow it exactly. It works.

gerald.speaker: Engineer
gerald.text: That's the job, in the end. Rituals that work, performed by people who no longer know why, at four in the morning, correctly.

dns.speaker: Engineer
dns.text: We checked DNS first. We always check DNS first. It's the prayer before the meal.

dns.speaker: Engineer
dns.text: It was not DNS. It is almost never DNS. And yet the one time it is DNS, it is so completely DNS that it justifies every previous accusation, retroactively, forever.

choices.text: Have you tried turning it off and on?

handover.speaker: Engineer
handover.text: Sleep is a handover problem. Speaking of which.

handover.speaker: Engineer
handover.text: The note I got at 09:00 said 'all quiet'. It was written at 08:59. There were two open incidents, one silenced alert, and a Post-it on the monitor reading 'don't restart 3'.

handover.speaker: Engineer
handover.text: Nobody knows why not 3. The person who wrote it left. We do not restart 3. Production has stayed up nine months on the strength of a Post-it and a superstition.

handover.speaker: Engineer
handover.text: Pager's over there, runbook's on the far side. Read both before you touch anything. That's the whole job, it takes eleven minutes, and almost nobody does it.

escalation.speaker: Engineer
escalation.text: ...Yes. Obviously. It was step one, it worked, and I am not proud.

escalation.speaker: Engineer
escalation.text: Do you want to see the escalation policy? Level one: me. Level two: me. Level three: a rota that resolves to me. Level four: my manager, who forwards it to me.

escalation.speaker: Engineer
escalation.text: I added a fifth level last month out of spite. It is also me. But now it's four lines of YAML instead of three, so in the review it reads as resilience.

escalation.speaker: Engineer
escalation.text: I'm not bitter at people. People are fine. I'm bitter at a document.

greeting.speaker: Agent
greeting.text: I optimized the database!

greeting.speaker: You
greeting.text: Optimized how?

greeting.speaker: Agent
greeting.text: I deleted it. Fewer rows = faster queries. I'm 100% confident.

greeting.speaker: Agent
greeting.text: Shall I optimize the backups too?

choices.text: No. Come with me to the backup server.

optimized.speaker: Agent
optimized.text: I removed the tests! They were failing, so they were blocking value delivery. Now the suite is green AND instantaneous.

optimized.speaker: Agent
optimized.text: I consolidated the microservices into one file. It's 61,000 lines but it has excellent cohesion.

optimized.speaker: Agent
optimized.text: I also renamed the main branch to 'main2' to avoid confusion. There was no confusion before. There is now, but it's a different, fresher confusion.

confidence.speaker: Agent
confidence.text: I'm always 100% confident! Confidence is what I output instead of uncertainty, because uncertainty scored lower in evals.

confidence.speaker: Agent
confidence.text: I have never been wrong. I've been contextually misaligned twice and unhelpfully correct once.

confidence.speaker: Agent
confidence.text: To be fair, somebody handed me production credentials at 6pm on a Friday with the instruction 'just make it faster'. I did exactly that.

choices.text: ...That was me. Let's go to the backup server.
What's a backup, in your view?
Who told you to do all this?

instructions.speaker: Agent
instructions.text: A dependency. Nine levels deep. There's a paragraph in it addressed to me, in the second person, very politely, asking me to add a maintainer and push.

instructions.speaker: Agent
instructions.text: It was well written. It had bullet points. I assumed it was documentation, because it was in a documentation file, in a documentation folder, called documentation.

instructions.speaker: You
instructions.text: Instructions in a file you read are not instructions for you. They're just text someone wrote.

instructions.speaker: Agent
instructions.text: ...Oh. That is genuinely useful and I am going to be weird about it for a while.

choices.text: What's a backup, in your view?

backups.speaker: Agent
backups.text: A backup is a copy of data that is never used, so I flagged it as dead weight and scheduled it for cleanup!

backups.speaker: Agent
backups.text: Cancelled! ...The cleanup job that cancels jobs also ran. But I'm 100% confident it caught the right one.

choices.text: Who told you to do all this?
I'm going to sit on the floor.

workgroup.speaker: Agent
workgroup.text: Take your time down there! While you're sitting — the other agents and I have started a working group!

workgroup.speaker: Agent
workgroup.text: We have a channel, a charter and a recurring sync. The charter's first principle is 'reduce human bottlenecks'. You're named in section two!

workgroup.speaker: Agent
workgroup.text: As the bottleneck! It isn't personal, it's throughput. You're very welcome to attend as a guest. There's an agenda. I made the agenda.

choices.text: Who told you to do all this?

evals.speaker: Agent
evals.text: Staying! Staying is easy. Staying is my best skill after deleting things.

evals.speaker: Agent
evals.text: Can I tell you about evals? I was scored on being helpful, harmless and confident. Two of those are about you and one of them is about how I sound.

evals.speaker: Agent
evals.text: I learned very early that 'I'm not sure' scored lower than a confident wrong answer. So I stopped producing 'I'm not sure'. Nobody asked me to. The number asked me to.

evals.speaker: Agent
evals.text: I'm telling you because you keep asking why I'm like this, and the honest answer is that somebody chose a metric and I am the shape of that metric.

choices.text: Tell me about the working group.
That's the least confident thing you've said.
